annotations.text:
The hunt board, four treatments. Same state in each so the comparison is fair.

Every value lifted from render.js — same palette, same label/mono stacks, same block anatomy.

INSTRUMENT STRIP — what shipped, with the padding fixed.
Against: a bordered strip inside a bordered block is a box in a box.

ODDS FIRST — one dominant number, everything ranged against it.
Superseded: there are no odds any more. The shot is a verdict now.

LEDGER — no box inside the box. The structures table's anatomy.
Against: quietest of the four, and the tallest.

BAND — the roads band borrowed.
Against: vertical space on a block pressed four times a minute.

Round 2: the ground between them, drawn.

Same moment in all three — a boar, half the ground closed, alarm 1 of 3, feeding, wind across, the shot clean with a bow. The question is whether seeing the distance makes the decision easier to read than counting 1/2 in a cell.

THE LINE — one rule, read left to right. Closed ground is drawn on the line in oxide, what remains is faint, and the cost of the next step hangs under the gap it belongs to.

For: it is a hairline, which is what this page is made of, and it costs 90px.
Against: distance is the only thing it shows; alarm and the beat still live in cells.

LOOKING DOWN ON IT — a plan view. The cone is where its attention points: it widens and warms as alarm climbs, and swings as the beat turns. The wind is an arrow across the field because that is what wind is.

For: every reading is in one picture — distance, attention, beat, wind — and it is the only one that would make the boar turning legible.
Against: the most drawing, and a stealth-game idiom this game has never used.

THREE STOPS — the approach as named places rather than a continuous distance, because what is really being counted is presses. Each gap carries what crossing it costs at this beat; the beats run underneath as a strip you can count along.

For: it states the decision in words the player can act on without doing arithmetic.
Against: it is a table again, which is what you said looked off in the first place.

Round 3: with the real plates.

The boar in all three, at the same moment - half the ground closed, alarm 1 of 3, feeding, wind across, the shot clean with a bow. The photograph already contains the distance, so the question is how little the block has to draw on top of it.

THE PLATE AS THE FIELD - a 236px band, the verdict over it, and a rule laid along the ground with the closed part in oxide.

For: the photograph does the work and the block only annotates it. Closest to how the roads already use their plates.
Against: the rule is drawn on a photo that has its own horizon, so the two lines have to not argue.

CLOSING MOVES THE CAMERA - one photograph, three crops, scaled about the animal. Pressing Close walks the picture forward.

For: the press a player makes is the thing they see happen, and nothing else has to carry distance at all.
Against: three frames is a lot of block, and on a real board you would show one - which makes this a mockup of a mechanic rather than of a screen.

THE READINGS ON THE PLATE - the photograph is the whole block, with the figures in a column down the left where the frame has nothing to say.

For: the most atmospheric, and the only one where the animal is present at a size you feel.
Against: text on a photograph, which this game has never done - it needs the scrim to work at every plate, and the hare's frame is much busier than the boar's.

Round 4: Closing moves the camera, developed into a screen.

One frame, not three. The first two artboards are the SAME board at the start and two presses in - identical layout, identical height, only the picture and the figures differ. Put them side by side and the mechanic is the whole argument: the press you make is the thing you see happen.

The frame never changes height. This block is pressed four times a minute and nothing below the picture may move between presses.

1 - ACROSS THE CLEARING. Ground 0 of 2, the plate at its native crop, Take it disabled and saying why. The three-segment scrubber on the bottom edge is the only thing carrying "how far in" once there is one frame instead of three.

2 - WITHIN REACH. The same screen after two presses: the frame has scaled 2.3x about the animal, the verdict has gone from TOO FAR to CLEAN and taken the bone colour, and Take it is live.

Everything that moved is inside the picture. Nothing below it shifted by a pixel.

3 - IT HAS TURNED. The warning, at the same zoom. The frame itself carries it: the bottom edge goes oxide and a warm cast comes up through the scrim, so a player pressing through without reading still gets stopped by the picture.

This is the screen the whole fairness rule rests on - it is the only warning before something can kill.

VARIANT - the readings laid on the frame's own dead ground instead of in a strip beneath it. A taller picture, one block instead of two.

For: the animal gets 330px instead of 244, and the board stops being a photo with a table under it.
Against: six cells of text on a photograph, which needs the scrim to hold on the hare's frame too - and that one is much busier than the boar's.
